name: Radioactive Mean Lifetime
description: Converts a radioactive half-life into the mean lifetime, th/ln(2). The mean lifetime is the average survival time of a nucleus and is always longer than the half-life. The result is in seconds.
notes: The mean lifetime is about 1.4427 times the half-life. Enter the half-life in seconds; the mean lifetime is the reciprocal of the decay constant.

name: Mean Lifetime from Decay Constant
description: Gives the mean lifetime of a decaying species as the reciprocal of its decay constant, 1/lam. It is the average time before a nucleus decays. The result is in seconds.
notes: The decay constant lam must be in 1/s. After one mean lifetime the surviving fraction has fallen to 1/e (about 37 percent).

name: Activity after Time
description: Computes the radioactive activity remaining after time t, A0·exp(-lam·t), where A0 is the initial activity and lam the decay constant. The result in becquerels follows exponential decay.
notes: The decay constant lam is in 1/s and t in seconds. Activity and number of nuclei decay with the same exponential; A0 sets only the initial scale.

name: Remaining Nuclei (Decay Constant)
description: Gives the number of undecayed nuclei remaining after time t, N0·exp(-lam·t), starting from N0 nuclei with decay constant lam. The result follows the exponential radioactive decay law.
notes: Enter lam in 1/s and t in seconds. The result is a count of nuclei; N0 must be the initial number at t=0.

name: Fraction Remaining (Number of Half-Lives)
description: Gives the fraction of a radioactive sample still remaining after time t, as 0.5^(t/th), where th is the half-life. Each half-life halves the remaining amount. The result is a dimensionless fraction between 0 and 1.
notes: t and th must share the same time unit, since only their ratio matters. The result gives the remaining fraction; multiply by 100 for a percentage.

name: Number of Half-Lives Elapsed
description: Computes how many half-lives have elapsed in time t, as the ratio t/th. This dimensionless count indicates how many times the sample has halved.
notes: t and th must use the same time unit; the result is generally not an integer. Raise 0.5 to this power to get the remaining fraction.

name: Q-value of Nuclear Reaction
description: Converts a nuclear mass difference dm (in atomic mass units) into the reaction Q-value, using dm·931.494 MeV/u. A positive Q means energy is released; a negative Q means the reaction is endothermic.
notes: The mass difference dm must be in unified atomic mass units (u); 931.494 MeV is the energy equivalent of 1 u. Use reactant minus product masses so that mass loss gives a positive Q.

name: Alpha Decay Q-value
description: Computes the energy released in alpha decay from the parent, daughter and alpha masses, as (Mp-Md-Ma)·931.494 MeV. A positive Q-value means the decay is energetically allowed.
notes: All masses must be in atomic mass units (u). Using atomic (rather than nuclear) masses is consistent because electron masses cancel in alpha decay.

name: Alpha Particle Kinetic Energy (Recoil)
description: Gives the kinetic energy carried by the emitted alpha particle in alpha decay, Q·(A-4)/A, after accounting for the recoil of the daughter nucleus of mass number A. The result is in MeV.
notes: A is the parent mass number, and the remaining fraction 4/A of Q goes to the recoiling daughter. This uses non-relativistic momentum conservation; enter Q in MeV.

name: Semi-Empirical Mass Formula (Binding Energy)
description: Estimates a nucleus's binding energy from the semi-empirical (liquid-drop) mass formula, combining volume, surface, Coulomb and asymmetry terms for mass number A and atomic number Z. The result is in MeV.
notes: This form omits the pairing term, so odd-even effects are not captured; coefficients vary between references. A and Z are integers and the result is the total binding energy.

name: SEMF Binding Energy per Nucleon
description: Gives the binding energy per nucleon from the semi-empirical mass formula, dividing the total liquid-drop binding energy by the mass number A. The result in MeV peaks near iron for stable nuclei.
notes: Omits the pairing term like the base formula; coefficients are model-dependent. Binding energy per nucleon indicates nuclear stability, highest around A=56.

name: Coulomb Energy Term (SEMF)
description: Computes the Coulomb repulsion term of the semi-empirical mass formula, 0.711·Z(Z-1)/A^(1/3), which reduces a nucleus's binding energy due to electrostatic repulsion among its Z protons. The result is in MeV.
notes: The Z(Z-1) form counts distinct proton pairs; some references use Z² instead. This term subtracts from binding energy and grows rapidly for heavy, high-Z nuclei.

name: Asymmetry Energy Term (SEMF)
description: Gives the asymmetry (symmetry) term of the semi-empirical mass formula, 23.7·(A-2Z)²/A, which penalizes nuclei with unequal numbers of protons and neutrons. The result in MeV reduces the binding energy.
notes: The factor (A-2Z) equals the neutron excess N-Z and vanishes for N=Z nuclei. This term subtracts from binding energy; the coefficient is model-dependent.

name: Surface Energy Term (SEMF)
description: Computes the surface-energy correction in the semi-empirical mass formula, which lowers a nucleus binding energy because nucleons at the surface have fewer neighbors. It scales as the nuclear surface area, proportional to A to the two-thirds power.
notes: The 17.8 MeV coefficient is an empirical fit and varies by parameterization. A is a dimensionless mass number; the term is a reduction of binding energy, so it appears with a minus sign in the full SEMF.

name: Geiger-Nuttall Law (log Decay Constant)
description: Estimates the base-10 logarithm of the alpha-decay constant using the Geiger-Nuttall relation, which links decay rate to the daughter atomic number Z and the alpha particle energy. Higher alpha energy gives a larger log decay constant and thus faster decay.
notes: Constants a and b are empirical and depend on the decay series; En is the alpha kinetic energy in MeV. The result is a base-10 logarithm of the decay constant, not the decay constant itself.

name: Nuclear Volume
description: Estimates the volume of a nucleus assuming it is a sphere whose radius follows R = r0 * A^(1/3) with r0 = 1.2 fm. The volume grows linearly with mass number A, reflecting the near-constant density of nuclear matter.
notes: A is the dimensionless mass number and the result is in cubic meters. The constant 1.2e-15 m (1.2 fm) is the standard nuclear radius parameter; other references use slightly different r0 values.

name: Nuclear Matter Density
description: Computes the mass density of nuclear matter by dividing the nuclear mass (mass number A times the atomic mass unit) by the volume of a sphere of radius r0 * A^(1/3). Because both mass and volume scale with A, the density is essentially independent of A.
notes: A cancels out, so the result is nearly constant at roughly 2.3e17 kg/m^3 for any nucleus. It uses r0 = 1.2 fm and treats nucleon mass as one atomic mass unit, ignoring binding-energy mass differences.

name: Coulomb Barrier (Fusion)
description: Calculates the Coulomb barrier height two nuclei must overcome to fuse, as the electrostatic potential energy of charges Z1 and Z2 at contact separation r0*(A1^(1/3)+A2^(1/3)). Higher charges or smaller nuclei raise the barrier.
notes: The result is in joules; divide by 1.602e-13 to convert to MeV. It uses point-charge Coulomb energy at the touching radius and neglects quantum tunneling that lets fusion occur below this energy.

name: Gamma-Ray Attenuation (Beer-Lambert)
description: Gives the transmitted gamma-ray intensity after passing through a material of thickness x, following exponential attenuation from the incident intensity I0. The linear attenuation coefficient mu sets how rapidly intensity drops with depth.
notes: mu and x must use consistent length units (here 1/cm and cm). This narrow-beam Beer-Lambert law ignores buildup from scattered photons, so it underestimates dose behind thick shields.

name: Half-Value Layer
description: Computes the half-value layer, the material thickness that reduces gamma-ray intensity to half, from the linear attenuation coefficient mu. It equals ln(2) divided by mu.
notes: Result units match the inverse of mu (here cm). Valid for monoenergetic narrow-beam geometry; for polyenergetic beams the effective HVL changes with depth due to beam hardening.

name: Tenth-Value Layer
description: Computes the tenth-value layer, the material thickness that reduces gamma-ray intensity to one tenth, from the linear attenuation coefficient mu. It equals ln(10) divided by mu.
notes: Result units are the inverse of mu (here cm). One TVL corresponds to about 3.32 half-value layers. Applies to monoenergetic narrow-beam attenuation without scatter buildup.

name: Photon Mean Free Path
description: Gives the photon mean free path, the average distance a photon travels before interacting, as the reciprocal of the linear attenuation coefficient mu. Larger mu means more frequent interactions and a shorter path.
notes: Result units are the inverse of mu (here cm). It represents an average; individual photon path lengths are exponentially distributed around this value.

name: Specific Activity
description: Computes the specific activity, the radioactive decay rate per gram of a pure isotope, from its half-life and molar mass. It combines the decay constant ln(2)/half-life with the number of atoms per gram from Avogadro number over molar mass.
notes: Half-life must be in seconds and molar mass in g/mol to give Bq/g. Assumes a pure single isotope; natural samples with mixed isotopes have lower specific activity.

name: Radiometric Age (Decay)
description: Determines the elapsed time since a sample formed from the ratio of initial to remaining amount of a radioactive nuclide, using its half-life. It inverts exponential decay: age equals half-life over ln(2) times ln(N0/N).
notes: N0 and N need only the same units since their ratio is used; half-life sets the output time unit (here years). Assumes a closed system with no gain or loss of parent or daughter besides decay.

name: Radiocarbon Age
description: Calculates a radiocarbon age from the ratio of initial to measured carbon-14 activity, using the 5730-year half-life of C-14. Age equals 5730 over ln(2) times ln(A0/Am).
notes: A0 and Am need only consistent activity units since the ratio is taken. This is the Libby-style decay age; calendar dates require calibration for past atmospheric C-14 variation.

name: Reaction Threshold Energy
description: Computes the minimum projectile kinetic energy needed for an endothermic nuclear reaction, from the reaction Q-value and the projectile-to-target mass ratio. The threshold exceeds the reaction energy deficit by the factor (1 + m/M) to conserve momentum.
notes: Meaningful only for endothermic reactions with negative Q; the absolute value of Q is used. This is the non-relativistic threshold in the lab frame, valid when kinetic energies are small compared to rest masses.

name: Nuclear Reaction Rate Density
description: Gives the number of nuclear reactions per unit volume per unit time as the product of target number density, reaction cross section, and incident particle flux. More targets, larger cross section, or higher flux all raise the reaction rate.
notes: Uses consistent SI units (targets per m^3, cross section in m^2, flux per m^2 per s) to yield reactions per m^3 per s. Assumes a thin target so the flux is not appreciably attenuated across it.

name: Macroscopic Cross Section
description: Computes the macroscopic cross section, the probability of interaction per unit path length, as the product of the number density of nuclei and the microscopic cross section. It represents the total interaction target area per unit volume.
notes: With number density in 1/m^3 and microscopic cross section in m^2 the result is in 1/m. It is additive over reaction types and isotopes when the corresponding cross sections are summed.

name: Neutron Mean Free Path
description: Gives the neutron mean free path, the average distance a neutron travels between interactions, as the reciprocal of the macroscopic cross section (number density times microscopic cross section). Denser material or larger cross section shortens the path.
notes: With number density in 1/m^3 and cross section in m^2 the result is in meters. It is an average for a single interaction type; combine cross sections for total interaction path length.

name: Neutron Flux Attenuation
description: Gives the neutron flux remaining after traveling a distance x through a medium, following exponential attenuation from the incident flux phi0. The macroscopic cross section Sig sets the rate at which flux is removed with depth.
notes: Sig and x must use consistent length units (here 1/m and m). This uncollided-flux form counts only neutrons that pass without interacting and ignores scattered neutrons returning to the beam.

name: Four-Factor Formula
description: Computes the infinite multiplication factor of a reactor as the product of the reproduction factor, thermal utilization, resonance escape probability, and fast fission factor. It gives the neutron multiplication per generation ignoring leakage.
notes: All four factors are dimensionless. This assumes an infinite medium with no neutron leakage; the effective multiplication factor also requires the fast and thermal non-leakage probabilities.

name: Six-Factor Formula
description: Computes the effective multiplication factor of a finite reactor as the infinite multiplication factor times the fast and thermal non-leakage probabilities. It measures whether the neutron population grows, holds steady, or shrinks per generation.
notes: All factors are dimensionless; a result of 1 means criticality. The infinite factor kinf here already bundles the four-factor formula, and the two non-leakage terms account for the finite reactor size.

name: Reactor Reactivity
description: Computes reactor reactivity, the fractional deviation of the multiplication factor from criticality, as (k - 1) divided by k. Positive values mean a supercritical, growing neutron population and negative values mean subcritical.
notes: The result is dimensionless and often expressed in dollars or pcm by scaling. Near criticality k is close to 1, so reactivity is approximately k - 1; small errors in k strongly affect it.

name: Absorbed Dose
description: Computes the absorbed radiation dose as the energy deposited by ionizing radiation divided by the mass of the absorbing material. One gray equals one joule per kilogram.
notes: Energy in joules and mass in kilograms give the dose in gray. Absorbed dose measures deposited energy only; biological effect additionally depends on radiation type and tissue, captured by equivalent and effective dose.

name: Equivalent Dose
description: Computes the equivalent dose by multiplying the absorbed dose by a radiation weighting factor that reflects the biological damage of the radiation type. It converts deposited energy in gray to a health-relevant dose in sievert.
notes: The weighting factor is dimensionless (about 1 for photons and electrons, up to 20 for alpha particles and neutrons). Numerically gray and sievert are equal, but they denote physically different quantities.

name: Effective Dose
description: Computes the tissue-weighted effective dose by multiplying the equivalent dose to an organ by its tissue weighting factor, which reflects that organ sensitivity to radiation-induced harm. The result expresses whole-body risk in sievert.
notes: The tissue weighting factor is dimensionless and the ICRP factors sum to 1 over all tissues. Total effective dose is the sum of this product over every irradiated organ, not a single organ alone.

name: Point Source Dose Rate (Inverse Square)
description: Estimates the dose rate from a point radioactive source as the dose rate constant times the source activity divided by the square of the distance. It follows the inverse-square law, so doubling distance quarters the dose rate.
notes: Units must match the dose rate constant (here GBq for activity, m for distance, giving mSv/h). Valid for an unshielded point source in air; it ignores attenuation and scatter buildup in intervening material.

name: Nuclear Magneton
description: Computes the nuclear magneton, the natural unit of nuclear magnetic moment, as the elementary charge times the reduced Planck constant divided by twice the proton mass. It sets the scale for magnetic moments of nucleons and nuclei.
notes: Uses the proton mass, unlike the Bohr magneton which uses the electron mass, making it about 1836 times smaller (roughly 5.05e-27 J/T). Mass in kilograms yields the result in joules per tesla.

name: Nuclear Magnetic Moment
description: Computes a nuclear magnetic moment as the nuclear g-factor times the nuclear magneton times the nuclear spin quantum number. It gives the magnetic moment along the spin axis in joules per tesla.
notes: The g-factor and spin I are dimensionless; 5.05e-27 J/T is the nuclear magneton. This uses the simple product form; the observable moment convention (maximum projection versus total) can differ by factors.

name: NMR Larmor Frequency
description: Computes the Larmor precession frequency of a nuclear spin in a magnetic field, as the gyromagnetic ratio times the field strength divided by two pi. This is the resonance frequency probed in nuclear magnetic resonance.
notes: Dividing by 2 pi converts the angular gyromagnetic ratio (rad per s per T) to an ordinary frequency in hertz. Use the angular gyromagnetic ratio here; some tables list gamma already divided by 2 pi.

name: Bateman Equation (Daughter Activity)
expression: N10 * lam1 * lam2 / (lam2 - lam1) * (exp(-lam1 * t) - exp(-lam2 * t))
description: Gives the daughter nuclide activity at time t in a two-step parent-daughter decay chain, using the Bateman solution. It combines exponential decay of the parent and daughter with initial parent nuclei N10 and the two decay constants.
notes: Requires distinct decay constants (lam2 not equal to lam1) or the formula diverges. Assumes no daughter present initially and a single parent-to-daughter branch; decay constants in 1/s and time in s.

name: Secular Equilibrium Daughter Activity
description: Gives the buildup of daughter activity toward secular equilibrium with a long-lived parent, as the parent activity times (1 - exp(-lamd*t)). The daughter activity rises and asymptotically approaches the constant parent activity.
notes: Valid only when the parent half-life greatly exceeds the daughter half-life, so the parent activity Ap is treated as constant. Decay constant in 1/s and time in s; at large t the daughter activity approaches Ap.

name: Fission Energy from Fuel Mass (U-235)
description: Estimates the total energy released if a given mass of uranium-235 fully fissions, by counting the atoms (mass over 235 times Avogadro number) and assigning about 200 MeV per fission. The result is the aggregate fission energy in MeV.
notes: Fuel mass in grams and 235 as the molar mass of U-235; 200 MeV per fission is a nominal average. It assumes complete fission of every atom, an idealization real reactors never reach.

name: Gamow Energy
description: Computes the Gamow energy, a characteristic energy scale governing Coulomb-barrier tunneling in charged-particle fusion, from the nuclear charges and the reduced mass of the pair. Larger charges or reduced mass raise this energy.
notes: Reduced mass in kilograms gives the result in joules; 137.036 is the inverse fine-structure constant and c is the speed of light. The Gamow energy sets the exponent in the barrier penetration factor.

name: Gamow Factor (Barrier Penetration)
description: Computes the Gamow factor, the exponential suppression of quantum tunneling through the Coulomb barrier, as exp of minus the square root of the Gamow energy over the relative energy. Higher relative energy gives a larger, less suppressed factor.
notes: EG and En must share the same energy unit since only their ratio matters. The result is a dimensionless probability-like factor between 0 and 1; it captures only the tunneling exponent, not the full reaction cross section.

name: Sommerfeld Parameter
description: Computes the Sommerfeld parameter, the dimensionless ratio of Coulomb interaction strength to kinetic scale for two charged nuclei, from their charges and relative velocity. It measures how strongly the Coulomb barrier suppresses low-energy fusion.
notes: The result is dimensionless; velocity in m/s. Larger values mean stronger Coulomb suppression and exponentially smaller tunneling, so slow, highly charged nuclei are hardest to fuse.

name: Neutron Diffusion Length
description: Computes the neutron diffusion length, the characteristic distance a thermal neutron diffuses before being absorbed, as the square root of the diffusion coefficient over the absorption cross section. Larger absorption shortens this length.
notes: Units must be consistent (here D in cm and Sa in 1/cm give cm). It is a diffusion-theory quantity for thermal neutrons; the mean square distance to absorption is six times the square of this length.

name: Reactor Period (Prompt)
description: Estimates the prompt reactor period, the time for neutron population to change by a factor of e, as the prompt neutron lifetime divided by (k - 1). A multiplication factor just above 1 gives a very short, rapidly growing period.
notes: Lifetime in seconds gives the period in seconds; the result is negative for subcritical k below 1. This prompt-only estimate ignores delayed neutrons, which in practice greatly lengthen the actual reactor period.

name: Nuclear Mass Defect
description: Computes the nuclear mass defect, delta_m = Z*mp + (A-Z)*mn - M, the difference between the summed mass of separate protons and neutrons and the actual measured mass of the nuclide. This missing mass corresponds to the nuclear binding energy via E=mc^2.
notes: All masses should be entered in atomic mass units (u). A larger mass defect means a more tightly bound, more stable nucleus.

name: Effective Half-Life
description: Computes the effective half-life of a radiotracer in the body, Teff = (Tphys*Tbio)/(Tphys+Tbio), combining radioactive decay with biological clearance. It is used in nuclear medicine to predict how quickly administered activity falls in a patient.
notes: Tphys and Tbio must use the same time unit, and the result shares that unit. The effective half-life is always shorter than either the physical or biological half-life alone.
